units.unitOverview: A force is a push or a pull, and once you can name the forces acting on something you can explain why it moves, why it stops, and why it stays exactly where it is. This unit names the forces you meet every day, shows that several always act at once, teaches you to draw them as arrows, and then looks at the one force that works without anything touching at all.
sources: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 5, topics on forces and magnetism
outcomes: Name the forces acting in an everyday situation.
Explain the difference between a push, a pull, and a force acting at a distance.
Recognise that an object at rest still has forces acting on it.
Draw a force diagram with arrows showing the name and direction of each force.
Tell a magnet apart from a magnetic material, and test which is which.
Describe how magnets attract and repel across a gap.
Compare the strength of two magnets fairly.

concepts.title: What a Force Does
concepts.explanation:
A FORCE is a push or a pull. That is the whole definition, and everything else in this unit is built on it. A force is measured in NEWTONS, written N, using a forcemeter - a spring that stretches further the harder it is pulled.

A force can do three things to an object, and only these three. It can make a still object start moving. It can change how a moving object moves - speeding it up, slowing it down, or turning it. And it can change an object's shape, which is what happens when you squeeze a ripe mango or stretch a rubber band.

Some forces need two things to be touching. An APPLIED FORCE is the push or pull you give something with your hand, a rope or an engine. FRICTION acts between two surfaces sliding past each other and always opposes the sliding, which is why a ball rolling on grass stops sooner than one on smooth concrete. AIR RESISTANCE and WATER RESISTANCE are friction with air and with water, and both grow the faster you move - which is why running feels harder into a wind and why swimming is slow work. A NORMAL FORCE is the push a surface gives back: the floor pushing up on your feet right now, which is the only reason you are not sinking through it. UPTHRUST is the upward push water gives anything placed in it, and it is why a bucket of water feels lighter under the surface than lifted out.

And one force needs no contact at all. GRAVITY pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth without touching it, which is why a dropped mango falls and why you have a weight at all.
concepts.example: A boy pulls a loaded cart along a dirt track. His hands give an applied force forward. Friction between the wheels and the track pushes backward. Gravity pulls the cart down, and the track pushes up on the wheels with a normal force. Four forces, on one cart, at one moment - and he can only feel one of them.

concepts.title: More Than One Force at Once
concepts.explanation:
Almost nothing ever has just one force on it. A book on a table, a boat on a lake, you on your chair - every one has at least two, and the interesting part is what happens when they are equal.

Take the book. Gravity pulls it down with, say, 4 N. The table pushes up on it with a normal force of 4 N. The two are the same size and point in opposite directions, so they CANCEL, and the book does not move. That is the important idea and it is easy to get backwards: the book is still NOT because no forces act on it, but because the forces that act on it balance.

The test is worth remembering. If you can think of a reason the object would fall, sink or slide, then there must be a second force stopping it. The book would fall, so something is holding it up. A boat would sink, so upthrust must be pushing it up as hard as gravity pulls it down. A parked lorry on a hill would roll, so friction must be holding it.

When the forces do not balance, motion changes. Add your hand to the book with a 2 N push sideways and nothing now cancels that push, so the book slides. Take the table away and the normal force goes with it, leaving gravity unopposed, and the book falls.

So 'balanced' does not mean 'still' and 'unbalanced' does not mean 'moving'. Balanced means the motion is not changing, which covers both a book sitting still and a canoe drifting at a steady speed.
concepts.example: Put a mango in a bowl of water and it floats, sitting lower in the water than you expected. Gravity is pulling it down and upthrust is pushing it up, and it sinks until the two are equal - then stops. Press it under with a finger and you have added a third force, and it moves again until you let go.

concepts.title: Drawing Forces as Arrows
concepts.explanation:
A force is invisible, and naming three or four of them in a sentence gets confusing quickly. Scientists draw them instead, and the drawing is called a FORCE DIAGRAM.

The rules are few. Draw the object simply - a box will do. For each force, draw an ARROW starting on the object and pointing the way the force acts. Label each arrow with the force's name. And if you know the sizes, make the arrows' lengths match them: a 10 N force gets an arrow twice as long as a 5 N one.

So the book on the table gets two arrows: one pointing down labelled gravity, one pointing up labelled normal force, both the same length because they are equal. The cart being pulled gets four. A falling stone gets one long arrow down for gravity and a short one up for air resistance.

The diagram earns its keep the moment you look at it, because balance becomes something you can SEE. Equal arrows in opposite directions mean nothing about the motion is changing. An arrow with nothing opposing it means the object will start moving that way. Two arrows the same way means a bigger effect than either alone.

One mistake is worth naming. Draw only the forces acting ON the object, not the forces it exerts on other things. The book pushes down on the table just as hard as the table pushes up on the book - but that push belongs on a diagram of the table, not of the book.
concepts.example: A diagram of a swimmer moving forward has four arrows: a long one forward labelled 'push from arms and legs', a shorter one backward labelled 'water resistance', one down labelled 'gravity' and one up labelled 'upthrust'. The forward arrow is the longest, so she is speeding up; the up and down arrows match, so she neither rises nor sinks.

concepts.title: Magnets and Magnetic Materials
concepts.explanation:
A MAGNET is an object that attracts certain metals towards it. A MAGNETIC MATERIAL is a material a magnet attracts. Those sound like the same thing and they are not, and the difference is the most-missed idea in this whole unit.

Hold a magnet near a steel nail and the nail jumps to it. The magnet is a magnet; the nail is a magnetic material. Now hold the nail near a second nail and nothing happens at all, because a magnetic material does not attract other things - it is only attracted BY a magnet. Every magnet is made of a magnetic material, and almost no magnetic material is a magnet.

Only a few materials are magnetic: iron, steel (which is mostly iron), nickel and cobalt. That is a short list, and everything else on Earth is not magnetic. This is the second common mistake - assuming all metals are magnetic. They are not: aluminium, copper, gold, silver and brass are all metals and a magnet ignores every one of them. A magnet is exactly how a recycling plant separates steel cans from aluminium ones.

And nothing that is not a metal is magnetic. Not wood, not plastic, not glass, not water, not paper. If a magnet picks something up, there is iron, steel, nickel or cobalt in it somewhere.

Every magnet has two ends called POLES, a north and a south, and they behave differently - which is the next concept.
concepts.example: A learner tests ten objects with a magnet: a steel spoon, an aluminium can, a copper wire, a plastic ruler, a glass marble, a coin, a nail, a wooden pencil, a rubber band and a paper clip. Only the spoon, the nail and the paper clip are attracted. All three are steel - and the aluminium can, which is certainly a metal, is not attracted at all.

concepts.title: Pulling Without Touching
concepts.explanation:
Every other force you can push with has to touch what it pushes. A magnet does not, and that is what makes it worth a unit of its own.

Bring a magnet slowly towards a paper clip on a table. Nothing happens, nothing happens - and then, while there is still a clear gap, the clip slides across and sticks. The force reached across the gap. It works through things too: a magnet will pick up a paper clip through a sheet of paper, a page of a book, a plastic ruler or a thin wooden board, because those materials do not block it.

The force gets STRONGER the closer the two are and weaker as they separate, which is why the clip lay still until the magnet was close. There is no sharp edge to it; it simply fades with distance.

And because a magnet has two poles, the force can go either way. Bring two NORTH poles together and they push apart - they REPEL. Two souths do the same. But bring a north near a south and they pull together - they ATTRACT. The rule is short: like poles repel, unlike poles attract. That is the only force in this unit that can push as well as pull without touching.

Repulsion is the better test of whether something is a magnet. A magnet attracts a magnetic material and it also attracts the other pole of another magnet - so attraction alone does not tell you which you are holding. Only another magnet will push back.
concepts.example: Float a bar magnet on a cork in a bowl of water and bring another magnet slowly towards one end. Turn the second magnet round and the floating one is pushed away instead of pulled in - it drifts off across the bowl. Nothing touched it either time.

concepts.title: Some Magnets Are Stronger Than Others
concepts.explanation:
Magnets are not all alike. A small button magnet off a fridge will hold one paper clip; a horseshoe magnet from the science cupboard will hold a chain of a dozen. MAGNETIC STRENGTH varies, and it can be measured rather than guessed.

There are two fair ways to compare two magnets. The first is to count how many paper clips each will hold in a hanging chain, clip to clip, until the chain breaks. The second, and the better one, is to find the greatest DISTANCE at which each will still start a clip moving: put a clip on a ruler, bring the magnet slowly along the ruler, and note the reading where the clip first twitches. A stronger magnet reaches further.

For either test to be fair, only the magnet may change. Use the same paper clips, the same surface, and the same way of measuring every time - and repeat each magnet several times, because where a clip first twitches is easy to misjudge by a few millimetres.

Strength is not the same as size. A small modern magnet made of special materials can easily beat a much larger old one. And a magnet can lose strength: dropping it hard, or heating it, jumbles the inside and weakens it, which is why magnets are stored in pairs with a small steel bar across the poles.
concepts.example: Two magnets are tested on the same ruler with the same clip. The fridge magnet starts the clip moving at 9 mm; the horseshoe magnet starts it at 41 mm. Each test is repeated three times and the readings agree within 2 mm, so the difference is real and the horseshoe magnet is far the stronger - even though the two are almost the same size.

explorations.title: Which Things Does a Magnet Pull?
explorations.context: To find out which materials are magnetic by testing them, rather than by guessing from what they look like.
explorations.prompt: Collect ten objects of different materials, including at least three metals that are not steel. Predict which will be attracted, then test each one with a magnet and record what actually happened.
explorations.answer: Only objects containing iron, steel, nickel or cobalt are attracted. Aluminium, copper and brass are metals and are NOT attracted, which is where most predictions go wrong.
explorations.hint: Sort your objects into two piles before you start - your predicted yes and your predicted no - and then test them. Comparing the two piles afterwards is where the surprise is.
explorations.explanation: Magnets and Magnetic Materials: only a few materials are magnetic, and being a metal is not enough. A magnet is exactly how a recycling plant tells a steel can from an aluminium one.

explorations.title: How Far Can a Magnet Reach?
explorations.context: To measure the distance across which a magnet can still act, and show that the force fades rather than stopping suddenly.
explorations.prompt: Lay a ruler flat with a paper clip at the zero mark. Slide a magnet slowly along the ruler towards it and read off the distance at which the clip first moves. Repeat three times and take the average.
explorations.answer: The clip moves while there is still a gap, and the distance is repeatable to within a few millimetres. A stronger magnet starts it moving from further away.
explorations.hint: Move the magnet very slowly near the end - a fast approach makes you overshoot the moment the clip first twitches.
explorations.explanation: Pulling Without Touching: the force reaches across a gap and grows stronger with closeness, which is why the clip lies still until the magnet is near.

explorations.title: What Is Holding It Up?
explorations.context: To show that an object sitting perfectly still has forces acting on it, by taking one of them away.
explorations.prompt: Rest a book on your flat palm and hold it steady. Describe what your hand can feel. Now lower your hand quickly and say what happens and why.
explorations.answer: The hand feels the book pressing down, and must push up just as hard to hold it still - two balanced forces. Remove the hand and gravity is left unopposed, so the book falls.
explorations.hint: Ask yourself what the book would do if your hand were not there. Whatever that is, some force must be preventing it.
explorations.explanation: More Than One Force at Once: a still object is not a force-free object. It is one where the forces cancel, and removing either one starts the motion at once.

methods.title: Drawing a Force Diagram
methods.example: For any object at rest or moving, draw the forces acting on it as labelled arrows and check whether they balance.
steps: Draw the object as a simple box.
Ask what would happen with no forces at all, and name the force that stops it.
Draw an arrow on the object for each force, pointing the way that force acts.
Label every arrow with the name of the force.
If you know the sizes, draw the arrows in proportion - a bigger force gets a longer arrow.
Check: equal arrows in opposite directions mean the motion is not changing.

methods.title: Comparing Two Magnets Fairly
methods.example: To decide which of two magnets is stronger, using a measurement rather than an impression.
steps: Put one paper clip at the zero mark of a flat ruler.
Slide the first magnet slowly along the ruler until the clip first moves, and read the distance.
Repeat twice more and take the average of the three readings.
Do exactly the same with the second magnet, using the SAME clip and the same ruler.
Compare the averages: the magnet that acts from further away is the stronger.
Say how much your three readings differed, so a reader knows how much to trust the comparison.

methods.title: Measuring a Force in Newtons
methods.example: To find the size of a pull using a forcemeter.
steps: Check the forcemeter reads zero before anything is hung on it.
Hang the object from the hook and let it come to rest.
Read the scale with your eye level with the pointer, not from above.
Record the reading in newtons, with the unit written down.
Repeat and average if the pointer is difficult to read steadily.

workedExamples.title: Naming the forces on a kicked ball
workedExamples.prompt: A football has just been kicked and is flying through the air. Name the forces acting on it now.
workedExamples.solution: Two. Gravity pulls it down towards the centre of the Earth. Air resistance pushes back against its movement, slowing it. The kick itself is NOT a force acting on the ball any more - that applied force ended the instant the boot lost contact.

workedExamples.title: Why a parked car does not roll downhill
workedExamples.prompt: A car is parked on a slope with its brakes on and does not move. What forces are acting, and what does that tell you?
workedExamples.solution: Gravity pulls it down the slope. Friction between the tyres and the road pushes up the slope by exactly as much, so the two cancel and the car stays put. The car is still because the forces balance, not because there are none. Release the brake and the friction drops, the forces no longer balance, and it rolls.

workedExamples.title: Is this object a magnet, or just magnetic?
workedExamples.prompt: A steel bar attracts a paper clip. How do you find out whether the bar is a magnet or simply a magnetic material?
workedExamples.solution: Bring a known magnet towards it and turn the known magnet round. If the bar is pushed away with one end of the magnet, the bar is itself a magnet - only two magnets repel. If it is pulled in whichever way round the magnet is held, it is a magnetic material and not a magnet. Attraction alone cannot tell you, because a magnet attracts both.

workedExamples.title: Reading a force diagram
workedExamples.prompt: A diagram of a falling stone shows a 6 N arrow down labelled gravity and a 2 N arrow up labelled air resistance. What is happening, and what happens next?
workedExamples.solution: The arrows do not balance: 6 N down against 2 N up leaves 4 N downward, so the stone is speeding up. As it goes faster the air resistance grows, so the up arrow lengthens. When it reaches 6 N the two balance and the stone stops speeding up, falling instead at a steady speed.

practice.prompt: What is a force?
practice.answer: A push or a pull.
practice.hint: The definition is only four words long.

practice.prompt: What unit is a force measured in?
practice.answer: The newton (N).
practice.hint: It is named after a scientist and is written with one capital letter.

practice.prompt: Name the force that pulls everything towards the centre of the Earth.
practice.answer: Gravity.
practice.hint: It is the one force in this unit that needs no contact at all.

practice.prompt: A book rests on a table. Name the two forces acting on it and say why it does not move.
practice.answer: Gravity pulls it down and the normal force from the table pushes it up. They are equal and opposite, so they cancel and the motion does not change.
practice.hint: Ask what the book would do if the table were not there.

practice.prompt: Give one difference between a magnet and a magnetic material.
practice.answer: A magnet attracts magnetic materials; a magnetic material is only attracted BY a magnet and does not attract anything itself.
practice.hint: Try holding two steel nails together and see what happens.

practice.prompt: Name three materials a magnet will NOT attract.
practice.answer: Any three of: aluminium, copper, brass, gold, silver, plastic, wood, glass, paper.
practice.hint: At least one of your three should be a metal, to show that being a metal is not enough.

practice.prompt: Two north poles are brought together. What happens, and what is the rule?
practice.answer: They push apart. Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
practice.hint: Two of the same always do the same thing.

practice.prompt: Why is repulsion a better test of a magnet than attraction?
practice.answer: A magnet attracts magnetic materials AND the opposite pole of another magnet, so attraction cannot tell the two apart. Only another magnet will push back, so repulsion proves it is a magnet.
practice.hint: Think about what a plain steel nail does when you offer it a magnet, either way round.

practice.prompt: A canoe drifts across a lake at a steady speed. Are the forces on it balanced or unbalanced?
practice.answer: Balanced. Balanced forces mean the motion is not CHANGING, which includes moving at a steady speed as well as standing still.
practice.hint: Balanced does not mean still.

practice.prompt: Describe a fair way to find out which of two magnets is stronger.
practice.answer: Use the same paper clip and the same ruler for both. Slide each magnet slowly towards the clip and record the distance at which the clip first moves, repeating three times and averaging. The magnet acting from further away is stronger.
practice.hint: Only the magnet may change between the two tests.

activities.title: The magnetic treasure hunt
activities.materials: One magnet, and twenty small objects from around the house of as many different materials as you can find.
steps: Sort the twenty objects into two piles: those you predict the magnet will pick up, and those you predict it will not.
Test each object and move any that surprised you into a third pile.
Look at the third pile and work out what the surprises had in common.
Write one sentence saying what all the attracted objects turned out to be made of.

activities.title: Magnet through the barrier
activities.materials: Two magnets, a paper clip, a sheet of paper, a plastic ruler, a thin book, a steel tin lid.
steps: Put the paper clip on a table and see how close the magnet must come to move it.
Now put a sheet of paper between them and test again. Then the ruler. Then the book.
Record which barriers made no difference and which weakened the pull.
Try the steel lid last, and explain why it behaves differently from all the others.

activities.title: Force arrows around the house
activities.materials: Paper, a pencil, and four everyday situations you can watch.
steps: Choose four things: something resting, something falling, something being pulled, and something floating.
Draw each one as a simple box.
Add and label an arrow for every force you can name on it.
For each drawing, write whether the forces balance, and say how you can tell from the arrows alone.

rules.text: A force is a push or a pull, measured in newtons (N).
Balanced forces mean the motion is not changing - which includes standing still AND moving at a steady speed.
Like poles repel, unlike poles attract.
Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic. Being a metal is not enough.

terms: A push or a pull, measured in newtons (N).
The unit of force, written N, measured with a forcemeter.
The force pulling everything towards the centre of the Earth, without touching it.
The force between two surfaces sliding past each other, always opposing the sliding.
Friction with the air, which grows the faster you move.
The upward push a liquid gives to anything placed in it.
The push a surface gives back to whatever rests on it.
Forces that cancel, so the motion does not change.
A drawing of an object with a labelled arrow for each force acting on it.
An object that attracts magnetic materials towards it.
A material a magnet attracts: iron, steel, nickel or cobalt.
One of the two ends of a magnet, north or south, which behave differently.
commonMistakes: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are. A magnet ignores aluminium, copper, gold and brass, which is exactly how steel cans are sorted from aluminium ones.
A still object has no forces on it.
It usually has at least two that cancel. A book on a table is pulled down by gravity and pushed up by the table by exactly as much.
Anything that a magnet sticks to is a magnet.
It is a magnetic MATERIAL. Two steel nails will not attract each other; only a magnet attracts, and only another magnet will repel.
The kick is still pushing the ball through the air.
The applied force ended the moment the boot lost contact. Only gravity and air resistance act on it after that.

connections.text: A magnet on the fridge door holds a note up because the door is steel. Try it on an aluminium window frame and it drops.
Anyone weighing produce on a hanging spring balance is measuring a force in newtons, then converting it to a mass in kilograms.
Drawing a force diagram turns an invisible push into something you can look at and check.
A steel can and an aluminium can look alike and are separated by a magnet in seconds.

realProblems.context: A loaded handcart is being pushed along a rough track and keeps slowing down whenever the pusher stops.
realProblems.prompt: Name the force that slows it, and give one thing that would make it easier to push.
realProblems.answer: Friction between the wheels and the track slows it. Better-inflated or smoother wheels, or a smoother track, would reduce the friction and make it easier.
realProblems.hint: The force that opposes sliding is the one that grows on a rough surface.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Friction is the force, and reducing it - smoother wheels or a smoother surface - is what makes the cart easier to push.

realProblems.context: A workshop floor is covered in a mixture of steel screws, aluminium rivets and plastic caps that all need separating.
realProblems.prompt: How would you separate them quickly, and which pile would still be mixed afterwards?
realProblems.answer: Sweep a magnet over the floor to lift out the steel screws. The aluminium rivets and plastic caps are both non-magnetic, so that pile would still be mixed and would have to be sorted another way.
realProblems.hint: A magnet answers one question only: is there iron, steel, nickel or cobalt in it?
realProblems.errorFeedback: A magnet takes out the steel screws in one pass, and leaves aluminium and plastic still mixed together.

realProblems.context: A shop sells two magnets at different prices and claims the dearer one is 'twice as strong'.
realProblems.prompt: Design a test that would check the claim, and say what result would support it.
realProblems.answer: Use the same paper clip and ruler for both, slide each magnet slowly in and record the distance at which the clip first moves, repeating three times and averaging. Keep everything except the magnet the same. A reading roughly twice as far for the dearer magnet would support the claim; a small difference would not.
realProblems.hint: A fair test changes only the magnet, and needs repeats before the difference can be trusted.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Same clip, same ruler, three repeats each, and compare the averaged distances - that is the only way the claim can be checked.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A mango hangs still on a branch. Explain why it does not fall, using the idea of balanced forces.
keyIdeas: Balanced, so the motion does not change
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: Gravity pulls the mango down, and the stalk holds it up with an equal and opposite pull. The two forces cancel, so the motion does not change and the mango stays where it is. When the stalk weakens and can no longer match gravity, the forces stop balancing and the mango falls.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: A friend says a magnet will pick up any metal. Explain what is wrong, and describe a test that would show it.
keyIdeas: Only iron, steel, nickel and cobalt are magnetic
Aluminium and copper are metals and are not attracted
Test several metals, not several objects
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: It is wrong because only a few metals are magnetic - iron, steel, nickel and cobalt - and most are not. I would test a steel nail, an aluminium can and a copper wire with the same magnet. The nail is attracted and the other two are not, although all three are metals. That one test settles it.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is a force diagram more useful than a sentence listing the forces?
keyIdeas: Balance becomes something you can see
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A sentence has to say which way each force points and how big it is, and a reader has to hold all of that in their head. A diagram shows direction by where the arrow points and size by how long it is, so whether the forces balance is something you can see at a glance instead of working out. It is also harder to forget a force when you are drawing the object.

questions.question: A force is best described as:
questions.hint: The definition is four words long.
questions.explanation: A force is a push or a pull, and it is measured in newtons.

questions.question: Force is measured in:
questions.hint: The unit is written with the letter N.
questions.explanation: Force is measured in newtons (N), using a forcemeter. Grams measure mass, not force.

questions.question: Which force acts without anything touching?
questions.hint: Three of these need two surfaces or a hand.
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls without contact. Friction, air resistance and an applied force all need something touching.

questions.question: Which of these is a magnetic material?
questions.hint: Only four materials on Earth are magnetic, and one of them is mostly iron.
questions.explanation: Steel is mostly iron, so it is magnetic. Aluminium and copper are metals and are not.

questions.question: A book lies still on a table. Which is true?
options: Two balanced forces act on it
Only the table pushes on it
questions.answer: Two balanced forces act on it
questions.hint: Ask what the book would do with no table.
questions.explanation: Gravity pulls it down and the table pushes up by exactly as much. The book is still because the forces cancel, not because there are none.

questions.question: Two south poles are brought close together. They will:
questions.hint: Two of the same behave the same way.
questions.explanation: Like poles repel. Only a north and a south attract each other.

questions.question: A steel nail will NOT pick up a second steel nail because:
options: it is a magnetic material, not a magnet
questions.answer: it is a magnetic material, not a magnet
questions.hint: Which of the two words describes the thing that does the attracting?
questions.explanation: A magnetic material is only attracted BY a magnet. It does not attract anything itself.

questions.question: A swimmer feels the water pushing back as she moves. That force is:
questions.hint: One of these pushes UP; this one pushes BACK.
questions.explanation: Water resistance opposes movement through water and grows the faster she swims. Upthrust is the separate upward push that keeps her afloat.

questions.question: A force diagram shows a 5 N arrow down and a 5 N arrow up. The object is:
questions.hint: Balanced forces say something about CHANGE, not about being still.
questions.explanation: Equal opposite arrows mean balanced forces, so the motion does not change. That covers standing still and moving at a steady speed alike - the diagram cannot tell you which.

questions.question: To compare two magnets fairly you must keep the same:
questions.hint: In a fair test, only the thing being tested may change.
questions.explanation: Everything except the magnet must stay the same, so the difference you measure is caused by the magnet and not by a heavier clip or a different way of reading the ruler.

units.unitTitle: Food, Digestion and a Healthy Diet
units.unitOverview: Food is the fuel and the building material for everything your body does, and it has to be broken down before any of it can be used. This unit sets out what a balanced diet actually contains, follows food on its journey from your mouth to the end of the line, names the organ that does each job along the way, and shows that most other vertebrates are built to the same plan.
sources: Cambridge Primary Science Teacher's Resource 5, topics on diet and on the digestive system
outcomes: Explain what a balanced diet is and name the main food groups.
Say why a diet short of one food group causes problems even when there is plenty to eat.
Name the organs of the human digestive system in the order food passes through them.
Describe the job each of those organs does.
Explain why food must be broken down before the body can use it.
Recognise that many other vertebrates have a digestive system built to the same plan.

concepts.title: What a Balanced Diet Actually Is
concepts.explanation:
Everyone knows a diet should be 'balanced'. The word is worth unpacking, because it does not mean eating a little of everything - it means getting enough of each thing your body needs for a different reason.

CARBOHYDRATES are the body's main fuel: rice, maize, cassava, bread, potatoes. They release the energy you move and think with, and they are the largest part of most meals. PROTEIN is the building material - beans, fish, meat, eggs, milk, groundnuts - used for growing and for repairing what is worn or damaged, which is why a growing child needs proportionally more of it than an adult. FATS AND OILS carry a great deal of energy in a small amount, and the body stores some for later and uses some to keep warm. VITAMINS AND MINERALS are needed in tiny amounts and are not optional: iron for blood, calcium for bones and teeth, vitamin C from fruit and vegetables. FIBRE cannot be digested at all, which is exactly its job - it gives the gut something to push against and keeps everything moving. And WATER, which is not food but is needed in the largest quantity of all.

BALANCED means having all of these in roughly the right proportions. That is why a person can eat a great deal and still be unwell: a diet of nothing but rice supplies plenty of energy and almost no protein, so a child on it may not be thin and will still grow poorly. The missing thing, not the amount, is what causes the harm.

The proportions shift with the person. A farmer doing heavy work needs more energy than an office worker of the same size. A growing child and a pregnant woman both need more protein, iron and calcium.
concepts.example: Two plates hold the same weight of food. One is all white rice. The other is rice with beans, a piece of fish, some greens and a slice of mango. Both give about the same energy, and only the second supplies protein to grow with, iron for the blood, calcium for the bones and vitamin C. Same quantity, entirely different meal.

concepts.title: Why Food Has to Be Broken Down
concepts.explanation:
Food on a plate is no use to your body, however good it is. The nutrients in it have to reach your blood to be delivered to your cells, and blood travels in vessels too narrow to see. So the food has to be taken apart into pieces small enough to pass through the wall of your gut and into the blood - and that taking apart is DIGESTION.

It happens in two ways at once, and both are needed. MECHANICAL breaking-up is physical: your teeth cut and grind, and the muscular walls of your gut squeeze and churn. That does not change the food chemically; it only makes the pieces smaller, which matters because it gives the second process far more surface to work on. CHEMICAL breaking-down is done by digestive juices, which act on the food and take large nutrient molecules apart into small ones.

So chewing is not politeness, it is the first step of the process, and it explains why food swallowed in lumps is digested badly.

One part of your food is never broken down at all. Fibre passes the whole way through unchanged, and that is its purpose: the gut's muscles need something solid to grip and push against, and without it everything slows and stops.

The whole journey, from the first bite to the end, takes most of a day.
concepts.example: Chew a mouthful of plain rice slowly and keep it in your mouth without swallowing. After a while it begins to taste faintly sweet. Nothing sweet was added - a juice in your saliva has already started breaking the starch into sugar, before the food has even left your mouth.

concepts.title: The Journey, Organ by Organ
concepts.explanation:
The digestive system is essentially one long tube from one end of you to the other, with a different job at each stage. In order:

The MOUTH. Teeth cut and grind the food into smaller pieces, and saliva wets it so it can be swallowed and begins breaking down starch.

The OESOPHAGUS. A muscular tube from the throat to the stomach, about 25 cm long. It does not simply drop food down - its walls squeeze in a wave behind each mouthful and push it along, which is why you could swallow lying down or upside down.

The STOMACH. A muscular bag that churns the food and mixes it with a strong acid and digestive juices. The acid also kills most of the germs you have swallowed. Food stays here a few hours and leaves as a thick soup.

The SMALL INTESTINE. A narrow coiled tube several metres long, and the place where almost all the real work happens. Digestion is finished here, and the small nutrient pieces pass through its thin wall into the blood, which carries them to every cell in the body. It is long and folded precisely to give a huge surface for that absorbing.

The LARGE INTESTINE. Wider and shorter. By now the useful nutrients have gone, and its job is to take back most of the remaining water, leaving the waste more solid.

The ANUS. The waste that was never digested leaves the body here.

Notice where digestion actually finishes. Most people say the stomach; it is the small intestine, and the stomach is a churning and softening stage on the way.
concepts.example: A mouthful of maize takes about a minute in the mouth, seconds in the oesophagus, three or four hours in the stomach, several hours in the small intestine where the goodness is taken out, and up to a day in the large intestine losing water. Nearly all the nutrition is removed in the middle stage, not the noisy one.

concepts.title: The Same Plan in Other Animals
concepts.explanation:
Your digestive system is not a human invention. Nearly every VERTEBRATE - every animal with a backbone - is built to the same plan: a mouth, a tube down to a stomach, a long intestine where absorbing happens, and an opening at the end.

Open up a fish, a frog, a chicken, a goat or a dog and you will find those same parts in the same order. That is a striking fact and it is worth pausing on: animals that live in water, in the air and on land, eating utterly different food, all process it with the same sequence of organs.

What varies are the proportions, and they vary with the diet. A goat or a cow eats grass, which is extremely tough and hard to break down, so its gut is enormously long - many times its body length - and it has extra stomach chambers, and it chews the food twice. A dog or a cat eats meat, which is far easier to digest, so its gut is short. A chicken has no teeth at all and swallows grit into a muscular gizzard that grinds the food instead.

So the plan is shared and the tuning is not. A long gut suits a plant eater and a short one suits a meat eater, and you can often guess an animal's diet from the length of its intestine alone.
concepts.example: A sheep's intestine, stretched out, is roughly thirty times the length of its body. A cat's is about four times. Both animals have the same organs in the same order, and the sheep needs far longer with its food because grass gives up its goodness so reluctantly.

explorations.title: What Is Actually on the Plate?
explorations.context: To find out whether the meals you eat in a day supply every food group, by recording them rather than remembering them.
explorations.prompt: Write down everything you eat and drink for one whole day. Then sort each item into carbohydrate, protein, fat, vitamins and minerals, or fibre, and say which group appeared least.
explorations.answer: Most days come out heavy on carbohydrate and lighter on fruit and vegetables. The point is not to score well but to see where the gap is, which is something only a written record shows.
explorations.hint: Include drinks and anything eaten between meals - those are the items people forget, and they often carry the most sugar.
explorations.explanation: What a Balanced Diet Actually Is: balance means having each group in roughly the right proportion, so the group that appears least is the one worth attention.

explorations.title: Chewing and Surface
explorations.context: To show why mechanical breaking-up makes chemical digestion faster, using something you can watch.
explorations.prompt: Take two equal lumps of sugar. Leave one whole and crush the other to powder. Drop each into the same amount of water at the same temperature and time how long each takes to disappear. Predict first.
explorations.answer: The powder dissolves far faster. Breaking the lump up did not change what it was - it increased the surface the water could act on, which is exactly what chewing does for digestive juices.
explorations.hint: Do not stir either one, or you will be testing your stirring rather than the surface.
explorations.explanation: Why Food Has to Be Broken Down: mechanical breaking-up gives the chemical stage far more surface to work on, which is why chewing properly matters.

explorations.title: How Long Is the Small Intestine?
explorations.context: To get a sense of a measurement that is hard to believe when you only read it.
explorations.prompt: An adult's small intestine is about 6 metres long. Measure 6 metres of string, then coil it into a space the size of your cupped hands. Write down what surprises you.
explorations.answer: Six metres coils into a remarkably small space, which is how it fits. The length exists to give a large surface for absorbing nutrients into the blood.
explorations.hint: Measure the string first and coil it afterwards - guessing six metres by eye is much harder than it sounds.
explorations.explanation: The Journey, Organ by Organ: the small intestine is long and folded precisely because absorbing needs surface, and that is where nearly all of it happens.

methods.title: Tracing the Journey of a Meal
methods.example: To name the organs of the digestive system in order and say what each does to the food.
steps: Start at the mouth and write down what happens to the food there.
Follow it to the next organ and name it before you describe it.
For each organ, write one sentence saying what it does TO the food.
Mark clearly the organ where digestion is finished and absorbing happens.
Check your order by asking whether anything you listed could come before the one above it.

methods.title: Judging Whether a Meal Is Balanced
methods.example: To decide whether a plate of food supplies what a body needs, and say what is missing.
steps: List every item on the plate separately.
Label each item with the food group it mainly supplies.
Look for any group with nothing against it.
Name one food that would fill that gap, available where you live.
Say what the body uses the missing group FOR, so the gap matters rather than just being a blank.

methods.title: Guessing a Diet from a Gut
methods.example: To use the length of an animal's intestine to work out what it eats.
steps: Find the length of the animal's intestine and the length of its body.
Divide the first by the second to get a rough ratio.
A ratio of about four suggests a meat eater; twenty or more suggests a plant eater.
Check your answer against what the animal's teeth are shaped for.
Say how confident you are, and why the two pieces of evidence agreeing matters.

workedExamples.title: Plenty of food and still unwell
workedExamples.prompt: A child eats large meals of nothing but rice and is not thin, but grows slowly and tires easily. What is missing and why does it matter?
workedExamples.solution: Rice is almost all carbohydrate, so there is plenty of energy and very little protein, iron or vitamins. Protein is the body's building material, so growth suffers, and iron is needed for blood, so the child tires. The problem is not how much food but which groups are absent.

workedExamples.title: Where does digestion finish?
workedExamples.prompt: Most people say food is digested in the stomach. Where is digestion actually completed, and what does the stomach do?
workedExamples.solution: Digestion is completed in the small intestine, which is also where the nutrients pass into the blood. The stomach churns the food, mixes it with acid and digestive juices, softens it and kills most swallowed germs - an important preparation stage, but not where the job is finished.

workedExamples.title: Why swallow food in small pieces?
workedExamples.prompt: Explain, using digestion, why chewing food properly helps.
workedExamples.solution: Chewing is mechanical digestion: it makes the pieces smaller without changing what they are. Smaller pieces have far more surface for the digestive juices to act on, so chemical digestion is faster and more complete. Food swallowed in lumps gives the juices less surface and is digested poorly.

workedExamples.title: Two animals, one plan
workedExamples.prompt: A goat's intestine is many times longer than a dog's. Both have the same organs in the same order. Explain both facts.
workedExamples.solution: The same order shows they share the vertebrate plan: mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus. The difference in length reflects the diet. Grass is tough and yields its nutrients slowly, so a goat needs a very long gut and extra stomach chambers; meat is far easier to break down, so a dog manages with a short one.

practice.prompt: Which food group is the body's main source of energy?
practice.answer: Carbohydrates.
practice.hint: Rice, maize and cassava are all in this group.

practice.prompt: Which food group does the body use for growing and repairing?
practice.answer: Protein.
practice.hint: Beans, fish, eggs and groundnuts are all rich in it.

practice.prompt: Name the organs of the digestive system in order.
practice.answer: Mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus.
practice.hint: Start where the food goes in and follow it all the way.

practice.prompt: What does the stomach do to food?
practice.answer: It churns the food and mixes it with acid and digestive juices, softening it and killing most swallowed germs.
practice.hint: It is a muscular bag, so one of its jobs is physical.

practice.prompt: In which organ is digestion completed, and what else happens there?
practice.answer: The small intestine. Digestion is finished there and the nutrients pass through its thin wall into the blood.
practice.hint: It is the longest part of the tube, and it is long for a reason.

practice.prompt: What is the job of the large intestine?
practice.answer: To take back most of the remaining water, leaving the waste more solid.
practice.hint: By this point the nutrients have already gone.

practice.prompt: Why does the body need fibre if it cannot be digested?
practice.answer: Not being digested is its job - it gives the gut's muscles something solid to push against and keeps everything moving.
practice.hint: Think about what the gut would have to grip without it.

practice.prompt: A person eats plenty of food and is still unhealthy. Explain how that is possible.
practice.answer: A diet can supply plenty of one group and almost none of another. Enough carbohydrate gives energy, but without protein the body cannot grow or repair, and without iron or vitamins other problems follow. Which groups are present matters as much as the amount.
practice.hint: Balance is about proportions, not quantity.

practice.prompt: Why must food be broken down before the body can use it?
practice.answer: Nutrients have to pass through the gut wall into the blood, and only very small pieces can. Digestion breaks the food down mechanically and chemically until the pieces are small enough to cross.
practice.hint: Think about where the nutrients have to get to.

practice.prompt: What does it tell you about an animal if its intestine is very long compared with its body?
practice.answer: It is probably a plant eater. Plant material is tough and gives up its nutrients slowly, so it needs a long gut and more time; meat eaters manage with much shorter ones.
practice.hint: Compare a goat with a dog.

activities.title: A day of food, written down
activities.materials: Paper and a pencil, and one ordinary day.
steps: Write down everything you eat and drink for a whole day, including between meals.
Label each item with the food group it mainly supplies.
Find the group with the fewest items against it.
Name one food you could actually get that would fill the gap, and say what the body uses that group for.

activities.title: Six metres of small intestine
activities.materials: String, a tape measure or metre rule, and a pair of cupped hands.
steps: Guess six metres of string by eye and cut it, then measure what you actually cut.
Cut a true six metres and coil it loosely into your cupped hands.
Write down how much space it took, and why the real one is folded rather than straight.
Explain in one sentence what all that length is FOR.

activities.title: The sweet rice test
activities.materials: A spoonful of plain cooked rice or a piece of plain bread.
steps: Put the food in your mouth and chew it slowly without swallowing.
Keep chewing for a full minute and notice any change in the taste.
Write down what changed, and when.
Explain where the sweetness came from, given that nothing sweet was added.

rules.text: A balanced diet has all the food groups in roughly the right proportions - it is not about quantity.
Food must be broken down small enough to pass through the gut wall into the blood.
Digestion is completed in the small intestine, not the stomach.
Most vertebrates share the same digestive plan; the proportions change with the diet.

terms: A diet containing all the food groups in roughly the right proportions.
The body's main fuel: rice, maize, cassava, bread.
The body's building material, for growth and repair: beans, fish, eggs, groundnuts.
A store of energy in a small amount, also used to keep warm.
Needed in tiny amounts and not optional: iron for blood, calcium for bones.
Food that cannot be digested, which gives the gut something to push against.
Breaking food down until its nutrients can pass into the blood.
The muscular tube that pushes food from the throat to the stomach.
A muscular bag that churns food with acid and digestive juices.
The long coiled tube where digestion finishes and nutrients enter the blood.
The wider tube that takes back most of the remaining water.
commonMistakes: Food is digested in the stomach.
The stomach churns and softens it. Digestion is completed in the small intestine, which is also where the nutrients pass into the blood.
A diet is what you do to lose weight.
A diet is simply what a person eats. Everyone has one, and the question is whether it is balanced.
If you eat plenty you will be healthy.
Quantity is not balance. A large meal of one food group can leave a body short of protein, iron or vitamins.
Fibre is useless because it cannot be digested.
That is exactly its job. Without something solid to push against, the gut's muscles cannot keep things moving.

connections.text: Adding beans to a plate of rice turns a meal of mostly energy into one that can also build and repair.
A nurse asks what a child eats, not just how much, because the missing group is what causes the harm.
A farmer feeds a goat differently from a dog, because a long gut and a short one need different food.
Writing food down for a day is a record, and a record shows what memory does not.

realProblems.context: A family eats well but the meals are almost entirely maize, with meat perhaps once a month.
realProblems.prompt: Which food group is short, and name two foods available locally that would fill the gap?
realProblems.answer: Protein is short. Beans, groundnuts, eggs, fish or milk would fill it, and several of those cost far less than meat.
realProblems.hint: The group that builds and repairs is the one maize supplies least of.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Maize is mainly carbohydrate, so protein is the gap - beans, groundnuts, eggs or fish would fill it cheaply.

realProblems.context: Someone eats very quickly, barely chewing, and often has stomach discomfort afterwards.
realProblems.prompt: Explain how chewing more would help, using what you know about digestion.
realProblems.answer: Chewing is mechanical digestion and makes the pieces smaller, giving the digestive juices much more surface to act on. Swallowed in lumps, the food is harder to break down and sits longer, which is uncomfortable.
realProblems.hint: Chewing does not change what the food is - it changes how much surface there is.
realProblems.errorFeedback: Smaller pieces mean more surface for the digestive juices, so chewing properly makes chemical digestion faster and more complete.

realProblems.context: A vet is shown an animal skeleton and an unlabelled preserved intestine, thirty times the animal's body length.
realProblems.prompt: What can the vet conclude about the animal's diet, and what would confirm it?
realProblems.answer: That it was almost certainly a plant eater, because plant material yields its nutrients slowly and needs a long gut. The teeth would confirm it: flat grinding teeth suit plants, and pointed tearing teeth suit meat.
realProblems.hint: Two independent pieces of evidence agreeing is stronger than either alone.
realProblems.errorFeedback: A gut thirty times the body length points to a plant eater, and flat grinding teeth on the skeleton would confirm it.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Explain how a person can eat a great deal of food and still not be healthy.
keyIdeas: Balance is about proportions, not amount
One group can be missing entirely
Each group has a different job
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: A balanced diet needs every food group in roughly the right proportion, and a large amount of one group does not make up for another being absent. Someone eating only rice gets plenty of energy but almost no protein, so the body cannot grow or repair itself properly, and little iron, so they tire easily. What is missing does the harm, not how much is eaten.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Why is the small intestine so long, and why does that length matter more than the stomach's size?
keyIdeas: Nutrients pass into the blood there
The stomach only prepares the food
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The small intestine is where digestion finishes and where the nutrients actually pass through the gut wall into the blood. Absorbing needs a large surface, and a long folded tube provides far more of it than a short one - which is why several metres are coiled into a small space. The stomach is a preparation stage: it churns and softens the food and kills germs, but nothing is absorbed into the blood there, so its size matters less.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: Most vertebrates have the same digestive organs in the same order, yet their guts differ in length. Explain both.
keyIdeas: Length is tuned to the diet
Plant food is harder to break down
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: The shared order - mouth, oesophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, anus - is the vertebrate plan, and animals living in water, air and on land all follow it. The length is tuned to what the animal eats. Plant material is tough and gives up its nutrients slowly, so a plant eater needs a very long gut and sometimes extra stomach chambers, while meat is easy to break down and a meat eater manages with a short one.

questions.question: Which food group is the body's main source of energy?
questions.hint: Rice, maize and cassava all belong to it.
questions.explanation: Carbohydrates are the body's main fuel and make up the largest part of most meals.

questions.question: Which food group does the body use for growth and repair?
questions.hint: Beans, fish and eggs are rich in it.
questions.explanation: Protein is the body's building material, which is why a growing child needs proportionally more of it.

questions.question: Which tube carries food from the throat to the stomach?
questions.hint: One of these carries air, not food.
questions.explanation: The oesophagus squeezes in a wave behind each mouthful and pushes it down - which is why you could swallow lying down.

questions.question: Which organ takes back most of the remaining water?
questions.hint: It comes near the end, after the nutrients have gone.
questions.explanation: By the large intestine the nutrients have been absorbed, so its job is recovering water and leaving the waste more solid.

questions.question: Digestion is completed in:
questions.hint: It is also where the nutrients enter the blood.
questions.explanation: The stomach churns and softens; digestion finishes in the small intestine, where the nutrients pass into the blood.

questions.question: Why must food be broken down?
options: so the nutrients can pass into the blood
so it can be swallowed only
questions.answer: so the nutrients can pass into the blood
questions.hint: Think about where the nutrients have to get to.
questions.explanation: Only very small pieces can cross the gut wall into the blood, and digestion makes them that small.

questions.question: Fibre is important because:
options: it gives the gut something to push against
it is the main source of energy
it kills germs in the stomach
questions.answer: it gives the gut something to push against
questions.hint: Its value is in NOT being digested.
questions.explanation: Fibre passes through unchanged, and the gut's muscles need something solid to grip and move along.

questions.question: A child eats large meals of only rice and grows slowly. The most likely reason is:
questions.hint: Which group does the body build with?
questions.explanation: Rice supplies plenty of energy and very little protein, and protein is what the body grows and repairs with.

questions.question: An animal's intestine is thirty times its body length. It most likely eats:
questions.hint: Which kind of food gives up its nutrients most slowly?
questions.explanation: Plant material is tough and slow to break down, so plant eaters need very long guts. Meat eaters manage with about four times their body length.

questions.question: Chewing helps digestion mainly because it:
options: increases the surface for digestive juices to act on
questions.answer: increases the surface for digestive juices to act on
questions.hint: Chewing is mechanical, not chemical.
questions.explanation: Chewing does not change what the food is; it makes the pieces smaller, which gives the chemical stage far more surface to work on.
